rv.q: This intimate, beautifully realized drama was Mr. McPherson’s breakthrough play, winning an Olivier Award after its London debut before arriving on Broadway in 1999.
Butler, Gormley and Keating inhabit their roles and chemistries with keen understanding, each actor having played his part for the company at least twice before.
Under Ciarán O’Reilly’s easygoing direction, it’s all delivered in a realistic flow that feels like an epic eavesdropping session in a pub.
The ensemble brings to life an exceptional play handsomely staged in a nice 148-seat theater, and that’s about as solid an Off Broadway experience as anyone can wish for this summer.
Whatever you think of the ghost stories themselves, this revival of The Weir certainly has terrific storytellers on hand to keep you riveted throughout.
It's about as fine a Weir as you'll ever see, rather like, well, spending 100 minutes in a rural pub with some engaging strangers trying to outdo one another in flights of lyrical fancy.
THE WEIR still manages to make us ponder what keeps us up at night while still leaving the door open to hope and possibility.
The play, now getting a pitch-perfect revival at the Irish Repertory Theatre under Ciarán O'Reilly's direction, celebrates the elemental pleasures of storytelling.
The play is brought to exhilarating life by a marvelous ensemble, under Ciarán O’Reilly’s assured direction.

Loneliness and tenderness suffuse 'The Weir.' Ultimately, it is a play about relationships and the human need for contact. One can’t expect much more than that from a theatrical experience. Under astute direction, the cast members project this rich mix of Irish and universal characters that stay with one long after the show has ended.
The astonishingly matter-of-fact, lived-in set created by Charlie Corcoran (Acorn’s Straight ) transports us to a remote little pub somewhere in the middle of Ireland.
Irish Repertory Theatre director Ciarán O’Reilly calls on a veteran cast to make the play palatable, and they do not disappoint...

Conor McPherson successfully raises the enduring questions about what makes us humans afraid and whether those fears are mostly about external events or the internal machinations of the mind and spirit.

cn.t: Irish Rep's fourth revival of McPherson's modern masterpiece earns high praise for its pitch-perfect ensemble and atmospheric storytelling, with critics celebrating the play's haunting exploration of loneliness and human connection in a vividly realized Irish pub setting.

vr.q: I liked the play enough that if I were in London this fall I'd honestly go see it again
